presenceLabel: Osage villages in Missouri (nothing drawn in Kentucky)
presenceNote: First documented: the Osage River villages on the 1673 maps of Marquette and Jolliet. Drawn: Osage River villages in western Missouri (Vernon and Bates counties) c.1673–c.1823, and the Little Osage in Saline County after 1717 (the county is uncertain). The Ohio Valley, including Kentucky, appears in Osage and Dhegiha Siouan oral tradition and in scholarship as the ancient homeland; no source gives a place or year in Kentucky, and scholars differ on when the westward move began. So nothing is drawn in Kentucky. Low–medium confidence.
overlapNote: Missouria, the Illinois Confederation (Cahokia and St. Louis area), Quapaw (Arkansas), Kansa and Caddo; later Cherokee and Chickasaw hunting; French, Spanish and American posts (Fort Carondelet 1795–1802, Lisa’s post 1802, Fort Osage 1808). No other mapped nation lies in this area.
basis: Osage Nation Historic Preservation Office, Missouri State Parks and the Historical Marker Database for Osage Village, the Oklahoma Historical Society, Wikipedia, and the 1808 treaty text. Oral tradition for the Ohio Valley origin. Mostly tertiary web sources plus one tribal-government page.

eras.label: c.1673–1716 · Osage River villages, Missouri
eras.text: On the 1673 maps of Marquette and Jolliet the Osage are shown south of the Missouri River, in the general location of the Osage River (Osage Nation Historic Preservation Office). Osage Village State Historic Site, in Vernon County, is the earliest known Osage village in western Missouri, home of the Little Osage and the Big Osage until 1717 (Historical Marker Database; Missouri State Parks). Principal villages stood where the Marmaton, Little Osage and Marais des Cygnes rivers form the Osage River, in Vernon and Bates counties. The tint is those two whole counties: a general area, not a boundary. 1673 is the year of the first European map, not a year of settlement.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · 1673 is a map date

eras.label: 1717–1785 · Little Osage move north; Big Osage stay
eras.text: After 1717 the Little Osage moved north, to Saline County according to Missouri State Parks and to ‘the Missouri River’ according to the Historical Marker Database. The Plattner Site, a Little Osage village in Saline County, is estimated to have been occupied from about 1717 to 1777 (National Register of Historic Places, quoted by Wikipedia). The Big Osage stayed on the Osage River, perhaps as late as 1775. The Saline County tint is one possibility, and its county is uncertain; the Osage River tint continues for the Big Osage. Both are general areas.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · Saline County is uncertain

eras.label: 1780s–c.1823 · Back on the Osage River until the move west
eras.text: A late Big Osage village west of Osage Village was occupied from about 1775 until the Big Osage left Missouri about 1823, and the Little Osage moved back to the area, probably in the 1780s, until they also moved west to Kansas around 1823 (Historical Marker Database). In 1808, at Fort Clark on the Missouri, the Osage ceded the land north of the Missouri and east of a line running due south from the fort; Fort Osage (Jackson County) and the 1825 Kansas reservation are text only and not drawn. The slider’s 1786 is a round number standing for ‘the 1780s’. The tint is Vernon and Bates counties: a general area.
